location: PDF p.501, sec 23.2.1 Path Planning on the NavMesh
quote: If a navigation mesh is available, each off-road segment is planned using this navmesh. verdict.objection:
The quote exists verbatim at the stated page and the scope objection does not apply (chapter 23 is entity-level ground vehicles; the cited sysdef paths are under simulationModelSets/EntityLevel), but the stated meaning has two defects.

(a) "Only the navmesh planner weighs soil/slope" is not stated. The text says the navmesh planner DOES weigh soil and slope; it never says no other component does, and p.508 contradicts the general form: the vehicle dynamics model weighs slope (throttle, sliding) and sec 23.5.1 weighs soil (acceleration/stopping factors) with no navmesh involved. An exclusivity claim that far requires inference the text does not license.

(b) The p.508 support is asymmetric and the finding states it as if symmetric. p.508 says only that GROUND SLOPE is not taken into account by the feature-obstacle planner. Whether the feature-obstacle planner accounts for SOIL is not stated anywhere I could find - so "which per p.508 ignores slope" is right for slope and the surrounding "soil/slope" framing silently extends it to soil.

Narrowly restated, the vendor chain the prereg wants does hold: no navmesh in the area -> off-road segments fall back to feature path planning (p.501) -> that planner does not account for ground slope (p.508). What does NOT follow is "the sim is slope-blind" or "only the navmesh weighs soil/slope" - slope-blindness is confined to path SELECTION on off-road segments, while slope and soil continue to act on the moving vehicle. Additionally the fallback covers off-road segments only; a Prefer-Roads entity's road segments were never navmesh-planned to begin with.

location: PDF p.502, sec 23.2.3 Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
quote: Note that the obstacle avoidance logic is choosing a direction to travel at every instant, but is not planning a path through the obstacles it sees. verdict.objection:
The quote is verbatim (modulo PDF space-stripping) and is entity-level ground-vehicle material (Chapter 23 "Ground Vehicle Movement"), so the citation itself is sound. Two over-reads in the 'meaning':

(1) "trapped by a large obstacle feature it cannot see around" is not what the text says. The text names two trap causes: a very large "alley" (an unqualified, undefined term - the guide never defines "alley", and it is a configuration of obstacles, not a single feature) and moving entities that close off its path. It does not say the trap is caused by one large obstacle feature, nor does it link the trap to "cannot see around" - the limited horizon and the lack of path planning are listed as separate properties of the avoider, and the "Therefore" is not decomposed into which property causes which trap. Saying the text describes "a large obstacle feature it cannot see around" is inference beyond the sentence.

(2) The trap statement is materially qualified by the immediately preceding section on the same page, 23.2.2 Move Execution (p.502), which supplies escape machinery not mentioned in the finding: "Ineitherkindofdriving,ifthevehiclebecomesblockedbyobstacles,itbacksupashortdistanceandattemptstodrivearoundtheobstacle.Ifbackingupfailsseveraltimes,thescriptmakesoneattempttorestartwithplanningfromitscurrentlocation." location: PDF p.505, sec 23.3 How the MoveAlongRoute Task Works
quote: The MoveAlongRoute task takes a route object and performs a sequence of movements directly to each vertex of the route. There is no path planning done as it moves toward the next vertex. However, the vehicle does avoid obstacles as it moves. If an obstacle causes the vehicle to move away from the path as it approaches a vertex, it will nevertheless consider that it has reached the vertex if it moves even with the vertex on a parallel path.
meaning: Confirms no re-planning occurs between STP-authored vertices, only reactive per-instant obstacle avoidance; also documents a vertex-arrival tolerance (parallel-path 'even with' counts as reached) that is unrelated to the stall symptoms but relevant to route-authoring semantics.

verdict.objection:
The quote is verbatim and correctly located, and it is entity-level ground-vehicle material (chapter 23 "Ground Vehicle Movement"; sec 23.5.1 points at ./data/simulationModelSets/EntityLevel/vrfSim/systems/movement), so check (3) passes. The core of the meaning - no path planning between vertices, obstacles avoided as it moves, vertex-arrival tolerance on a parallel path - does follow. But three parts of the stated meaning do not:
1. "only reactive per-instant obstacle avoidance" - "per-instant" is not stated. The text says only "the vehicle does avoid obstacles as it moves"; it says nothing about the time granularity or the mechanism of that avoidance.
2. "unrelated to the stall symptoms" is an unsupported editorial claim, and it is contradicted in spirit by the very next sentence the finding drops: MoveAlongRoute constrains the vehicle's speed to keep it following the route ("itsspeedisconstrainedtoensurethatitfollowstheroutereasonablywelleveniftheroutecurves"). For an investigation into slow/crawling movement, that sentence is the most load-bearing one on the page and the finding omits it while asserting irrelevance to stalls. Not stated either way - so "unrelated" should not be asserted.
3. The "no re-planning" generalization is unqualified in the finding but is qualified in the document: if the MoveAlongRoute task carries Treat Route as Road (sec 23.2.4, p.503), road-driving behavior applies - a travel path is constructed through intersections and the vehicle follows lane centerlines exactly and will NOT move aside to avoid an obstacle. So both halves of the quoted claim (no planning; does avoid obstacles) flip under that option.
4. Minor: "STP-authored" is the finding's framing; the Users Guide says nothing about STP. Harmless if read as "the vertices as authored", but it is not in the text.
Recommend rewording the meaning to: "MoveAlongRoute moves directly vertex-to-vertex with no path planning toward the next vertex, avoids obstacles while moving, counts a vertex as reached when the vehicle draws even with it on a parallel path, and constrains speed so the route is followed reasonably well through curves - all for the non-road case; Treat Route as Road switches to road-driving semantics (constructed travel path, exact lane centerline following, no lateral obstacle avoidance)."

This is a documented speed constraint imposed by MoveAlongRoute itself. (2) Sec 23.2.4 "Vehicle Movement On Roads", p.503: "Roaddrivingisvalidonlyforgroundvehicles.Ifyougiveamovementtaskwitharoaddrivingelement(includingTreatRouteasRoadinaMoveAlongRoutetask,orPreferRoadsinaspawnpattern'sdefaultplan)toanyothertypeofentity,itwillfail." and, for road driving, p.503: "Vehiclesonroadsfollowthelanecenterlinesexactly.Vehicleswillnevermovetoonesideofthelaneortheothertoavoidanobstacle,forexample." verdict.objection:
Quote is verbatim at the stated location and the subject matter is entity-level ground vehicle units, so no objection on scope-of-domain. Three over-reads in the "meaning":

(1) "not a wait-state or task hold" is inferred from silence. The text says the leader/followers "use speed control to remain within some distance of each other"; it does not say speed control is the ONLY mechanism, and it does not deny a hold/wait. The finding's own next clause concedes the Guide is silent - silence cannot simultaneously support an exclusion claim. Positive support for "speed control is A mechanism" holds; "not a wait-state" does not.

(2) Scope creep from "Maneuver Along" to "a unit's Move-Along/Maneuver-Along task". Sec 30.22 governs Maneuver Along (and 30.23 Maneuver To, identical wording). For Move Along Route on a unit, p.600 says subordinates "may use the Maneuver Along subtask... for example, individual vehicles or ground vehicle subunits that are configured to use Maneuver Along", while subordinates not equipped with ground vehicle maneuver tasks (e.g. humans) "execute the move-along task as described above". So the speed-control mechanism attaches to Move Along Route only conditionally, per subordinate configuration - not as "the vendor's coordination mechanism for a unit's Move-Along task".

(3) The omitted qualifier "speedcontrolcanoverrideorderedspeed" is material and, if anything, strengthens the mechanism claim but also bounds it: the doc frames speed control as acting on ordered speed, saying nothing about a floor at zero. Also omitted is the weaker framing "makinganattempttoremaintogetherinsomeformation" - the Guide's commitment is an attempt, not a guarantee, which is exactly the gap the finding wants to exploit but does not quote.

(4) The negative claim "The Guide never states what happens when a follower's speed cannot be reduced further" is a whole-document claim verified here only by a targeted scan of pages containing "speed control", "waits for", "catch up", "falls behind", "remain together" (pp. 504, 566, 568, 588, 594, 598, 599, 906, 945). So: not refuted, but stated more strongly than the evidence gathered supports - it should read "not stated in sec 30.22/30.23 nor in the speed-control/catch-up passages found elsewhere".

location: PDF p.517, sec 25.2 How Units Move
quote: When a unit receives a movement command, VR-Forces calculates the path the unit leader must follow to reach the destination. It then calculates offset destinations for each subordinate in the unit as well as the routes to those destinations, which are offset from the leader's route.
meaning: Background confirming each member gets its own offset route computed once at task issue, consistent with the prereg's observation that one lane's terrain can trap a single offset route while neighboring lanes pass.

verdict.objection: Check (1) passes: the quote is verbatim (spacing lost) on p.517, sec 25.2, and check (3) passes: chapter 25 is explicitly entity-level, and the surrounding subsection 25.2.2 is "GroundVehicleUnitMovement", so ground vehicles/units are in scope. Check (2) fails on two words of the meaning. (a) "computed once at task issue" - the text says only that the calculation happens "When a unit receives a movement command"; it never says the routes are computed once, are static, or are not recomputed. The neighbouring text pulls the other way: formation IDs are reassigned dynamically when members are destroyed/removed/independently tasked (p.517 "ClosingFormation"), the offsets are tied to "theunit'scurrentformation" (a mutable state), and p.518 says the unit-level controller "ultimatelysendstaskstoitsindividualsubordinates" - i.e. ongoing task issuance, not a one-shot plan. The text also defers per-task detail to Chapter 30 (p.583), so 25.2 is explicitly not the authoritative account of how movement is performed. (b) "one lane's terrain can trap a single offset route while neighboring lanes pass" - terrain, obstacles, failure, stalling, and per-member independence of failure are not stated anywhere in 25.2; nothing in the passage says a subordinate route can fail, or that a subordinate's failure does not propagate to the unit. That is inference, not text. - The failure sentence is listed as a DISADVANTAGE OF USING SECTORS, not as an argument for them. location: PDF p.483, sec 21.9.1 Setting the Notification Level for Console Messages

verdict.objection:
The quote is verbatim (allowing lost spaces and the en-dash rendered as "-"/"?"), at the stated location, and the scale + "default notification level is 2" half of the meaning holds exactly. The rest does not follow from the text:

Level 2 is described as printing "Somediagnosticinformation ... withwarningsandfatalmessages"; the guide does not say what "some" covers, so it cannot support "path plans and stall loops would likely not appear". Notably, a stall/failure message could well be a warning or fatal message, which prints at level 1 and even level 0. The doc equally permits "the needed messages DO appear at 2" - so it does not establish the claimed "plain-vendor-default explanation for almost silent consoles".

3. Two qualifiers weaken the default-2 framing: the level is set PER OBJECT (so "the default" is per-object, not a run-wide setting), and NotifyLevel cannot be set from the Object Console for REMOTE simulated objects (objects simulated by another application) - directly relevant to a bridge/observer setup where the objects of interest may be remote.

4. Scope: sec 21.9 is generic to "simulationobjectsandtacticalgraphics", not specific to entity-level ground vehicles/units (it explicitly extends to aggregate-level combat-engineering objects at 40.55, p.890). verdict.objection: Three objections. (1) Over-read of "forever": the text says entity A keeps looking "until entity B becomes available, or until entity A is assigned another task", and the preceding bullets add override and destruction of the followed entity as terminators. "Indefinite retry" with no qualifier is stronger than the text; "retries forever" is contradicted by the enumerated exits. (2) False parallel: the finding contrasts this with "Move to Altitude gives up and reports". Sec 30.29 p605 says nothing about giving up when a target cannot be found - it says a fixed-wing entity ON THE GROUND cannot respond, prints a console message, and ignores the task. That is a platform-capability precondition, not a search/acquisition failure. Comparing the two yields the generalization "the vendor does not have one uniform give-up policy across task types", which is inference the text does not state - neither section makes any cross-task claim. Not stated. (3) Scope: the quote is entity-level (Chapter 30 is titled "Movement Tasks for Entity-Level Scenarios"), and Follow Entity is not restricted by platform in the assign steps, so it does cover ground vehicles. But the other half of the contrast, Move to Altitude, is explicitly aircraft-only ("You can order an aircraft entity to move to an altitude", p605), so the asserted contrast is not an entity-level-ground-vehicle statement at all. The quote itself is admissible; the "meaning" attached to it is not.
verdict.context_that_changes_it: Immediately above the quote, p593-594 lists the terminating conditions: "An entity continues to follow its target entity until: [l] The task is overridden. [l] The followed entity is destroyed." So the retry is not unbounded - it ends on override, reassignment, or destruction of the target. The claimed counter-example, sec 30.29 p605, reads: "Fixed-wing entities that are on the ground cannot respond to a Move to Altitude task. If they are given this task, a message prints to the object console and the entity ignores the task." That is an ineligible-platform rejection at task assignment, not a "target cannot be found" case - the two texts are not describing the same situation.

quote: PruneNo-GoTerrainAreas: Do not calculate navigation data for areas in which simulation objects cannot move.

The quote is verbatim and correctly located, but the 'meaning' adds two things the text does not say.

(1) "rather than leaving it in as unreachable nodes" is NOT STATED. Table 54 says only what the option does when ON ("Do not calculate navigation data for areas in which simulation objects cannot move"); the guide says nothing on p.1279 (or the surrounding 66.2.2 / 66.3 text on pp.1276-1281) about what the graph contains when the option is OFF - "unreachable nodes" is the verifier's invention. (2) "generation-time filter, not a runtime obstacle report" is half-supported and half-over-read. Table 54 describes the fields in the dialog box.") and it governs navigation-data calculation (sec 66.3, p.1281: "To generate navigation data, you create navigation areas and then generate navigation data for them."). The quote is genuine and correctly located, but the 'meaning' asserts three things the sentence does not say.

(1) "outside any area ... it falls back to standard navigation" is NOT stated. The text says standard navigation applies "if they move between them" - i.e. movement BETWEEN navigation areas. It says nothing about an entity operating outside/without any navigation area. Not stated.

(2) "standard (feature-obstacle) navigation" - the guide never defines "standard navigation" anywhere else; a full-text scan of the 1806-page Users Guide finds the phrase "standard navigation" ONLY on p.1281. Also note a stronger, uncited time claim immediately after the quote on the same page, which the finding omits: "MAKhasrecordedthistakingoneweektofinishonamaximumsizenavigationarea" (cover-point calculation for lifeforms).

2. "not slope, soil, or vehicle-blocked conditions" - category error, and partly contradicted. dynamic-terrain-type values name types of terrain CHANGE; slope/soil are static terrain attributes handled at generation time. p.1282 explicitly documents soil handling via soil-types-to-tag-with-surface-char, and p.1285 notes lifeforms "can move on steeper surfaces than ground platforms" - i.e. slope and soil ARE navigation inputs, just not regeneration triggers. This is the vendor's own code, not an inference: a ground vehicle that is still blocked after one global replan parks itself forever inside this loop node with no further recovery attempt from the script.

verdict.objection:
The quote is verbatim at the stated lines (whitespace aside), and it is entity-level ground-vehicle code (EntityLevel/scripts/ground-vehicle-move-to.lua), so check (3) passes. The MEANING is wrong on two counts.

(1) The entry condition is inverted. The finding says the stall is entered "when exactly one global replan has already been attempted". The sequence's first child is the opposite gate (:1267-1272): hasNotAttemptedGlobalReplanning = {nodeType = "condition", name = "Has not attempted global replanning?", condition = function(node) return not getStateVar("globalReplanAttempted") end}. A Lua sequence stops at a failing child, so once globalReplanAttempted is true the sequence FAILS at that condition and loopToStall is never reached. The stall is entered only on the first global replan, i.e. when none has yet been attempted.

(2) "No further recovery attempt / parks itself forever" is not stated and is contradicted by the node it follows. So the vendor's own naming ("stall FOR replanning") and wiring say the loop holds this branch while a replan is issued; whether the branch is ever exited depends on behaviorEngine tick/selector semantics, which this file does not state. Also, the parent selector carries an escape the finding omits (:1294-1301): loopOrReplanOnce = {... failWhen = function(node) return getStateVar("PathPlanFailure") end}.

Nothing in the file says the entity is stuck forever with no recovery; that is inference layered on a node name. verdict.objection:
The quote is accurate but the reading is wrong in two places, one of them inverted.

(1) INVERTED: "a second blockage ... falls straight to the stall loop above." loopToStall is the THIRD child of the SEQUENCE attemptGlobalReplanningOnce (lines 1288-1291): children = { hasNotAttemptedGlobalReplanning, globalReplan, loopToStall }. In a sequence the stall loop is reached only AFTER the condition succeeds - i.e. on the FIRST blockage-driven replan. Once globalReplanAttempted is latched, the condition fails at line 1269, the sequence fails immediately, and loopToStall is never entered; the fallback selector loopOrReplanOnce (lines 1292-1300, children {loopOverPathParts, attemptGlobalReplanningOnce}) then has both children failed. What the text supports is "no second global replan"; it does NOT support "falls into the stall loop."

(2) OVER-STATED: "set the first (and only) time a full replan runs." The latch is set only on the replan-flag branch (line 1327-1331, i.e. blockage-driven, flag set at line 1275). The destination-change branch (lines 1333-1338: "if dist > LOCATION_CHANGE_THRESHOLD then replanNow = true; setStateVar('lastDestinationLocation', ...)") sets replanNow WITHOUT touching globalReplanAttempted, and so does the "no path yet" branch (1324-1326). So full replans can and do run without setting or being blocked by the latch - the latch caps only blockage-driven global replans.

(3) PARTLY SUPPORTED WITH QUALIFIERS: "never cleared for the life of the task" - within this file globalReplanAttempted is written only at line 1330 and read only at line 1269 (grep: no other occurrences), so it is never cleared HERE; but setStateVar/getStateVar are engine-provided (no "function setStateVar" anywhere under C:\MAK\vrforces5.2d\data), so the variable's lifetime/scope is NOT STATED by the text - "for the life of the task" is an assumption.

(4) "no periodic/timed re-plan of a route already in progress" is defensible for a global replan (only triggers in isDestChanged are: MultiPartPath == nil, the replan flag, and distance > LOCATION_CHANGE_THRESHOLD = 1.0, line 44), but the neighbouring text qualifies it: the route in progress IS locally re-routed repeatedly without any of these - maybeSkirtABlock (lines 1201-1208) with incrementReplanAttempts and testBackupAttemptLimit, and the skirt code splices new parts into MultiPartPath at lines 1090-1093 and 1130-1133. So "no re-plan" must be narrowed to "no global re-plan"; local blockage skirting recurs up to a backup-attempt limit.

-- The script automatically tries to plan a path using road features
-- unless navigation preferences are set to Ignore Roads.
-- In the sections of the route that are off-road, the script uses
-- navigation meshes if they are available. Otherwise, it uses the feature
-- path planner to plan a path around obstacle features. ... maybePlanOffroadNavPath = {... children = { isRoadFollowingDisabled , isCurrentPointInNavArea , isDestInNavArea , createOffroadSegment , calcOffroadNavPath , markNoRoadNavPathPlanned } } ... selectPlanTechnique = {nodeType = "selector", ... children = { maybePlanOffroadNavPath , planOffroadFeatPath } }
meaning: Confirms, from the script itself (not just the User's Guide), exactly when the nav mesh is used for a given leg: only when BOTH the vehicle's current point AND the destination are inside a nav area (isCurrentPointInNavArea and isDestInNavArea both true). If either endpoint of that leg is outside a nav area, the selector falls back to the feature-obstacle planner (planOffroadFeatPath, using vrf:computePathThroughFeatures). A route that crosses in and out of a nav area therefore silently switches planners leg by leg.

verdict.objection:
Scope check (3) passes: this is the EntityLevel scripted task for ground vehicles ("This is the scripted task that ground vehicles use for all movement to a specified location.", line 1-2). The quote is verbatim: header lines 5-9, maybePlanOffroadNavPath at 1461-1470, selectPlanTechnique at 1570-1581.

The MEANING fails on two counts.

(a) It drops a mandatory precondition that is present in the very children list it quotes. maybePlanOffroadNavPath is a "sequence" whose FIRST child is isRoadFollowingDisabled (line 1463), defined at 1410-1414: 'condition = function(node) return not this:getInternalStateProperty("Movement", "UseRoads") end'. A sequence fails at its first failing child, so at this node the nav mesh is reached ONLY when road following is disabled. The finding says the gate is "only when BOTH the vehicle's current point AND the destination are inside a nav area" - that is necessary but not sufficient. With UseRoads true (the default posture the header describes: "The script automatically tries to plan a path using road features unless navigation preferences are set to Ignore Roads."), this branch fails immediately and planOffroadFeatPath runs regardless of nav areas.

(b) "for a given leg" / "switches planners leg by leg" is not stated and is contradicted by what the cited conditions actually read. isCurrentPointInNavArea tests 'isPointInNavArea(this:getLocation3D())' (line 1418) - the entity's current position - and isDestInNavArea tests 'isPointInNavArea(taskParameters.destination:getLocation3D())' (line 1424) - the single task destination, not a route leg. selectPlanTechnique sits inside maybePlanPath (lines 1583-1592) behind isDestChanged, i.e. it is a one-shot, whole-task planner choice. This file is move-to only; header line 3: "(Other tasks handle move-along route, follow-entity, etc.)".

Per-part nav-mesh selection DOES exist in this file, but at a DIFFERENT node the finding did not cite: maybeMakeNavPath, lines 472-545, whose isPathPartOutsideNavArea (478-483) reads 'return (not isPointInNavArea(part.segments[1])) or (not isPointInNavArea(part.end_location))' on the ACTIVE PathPart, with calcOffroadNavPath (485-502) calling 'vrf:findPathToLocation(part.segments[1], part.end_location, params)'. That is where an off-feature segment of an already road-planned multi-part path gets a nav path or not. If the finding wants the leg-by-leg claim, it must be re-anchored to 472-545, and even there the fallback is "continue with feature planned-path" (comment at 542-543), not a re-entry into planOffroadFeatPath.

Minor: "silently" is not supported - calcOffroadNavPath's exitFn emits printInfo("Planned nav path is nil.") / "has not enough ... points." (lines 505-508).

Verified: vrf:computePathThroughFeatures is indeed what planOffroadFeatPath -> planPath calls (line 1381). Not stated anywhere in the file: that a route crossing in and out of a nav area switches planners per leg.

verdict.objection: The quote is real and the parameter list is complete (the vendor luadoc lists exactly those six fields), so "no slope or soil argument" is supported. Three things break the stated meaning: (1) "no ... elevation ... argument anywhere" is false on the face of the quote - start and destination are getLocation3D(), i.e. 3D, elevation-bearing arguments; the doc types them "Location3D". (2) "the planner ... has no slope input at all" does not follow. The call is an async job dispatched into the C++ engine ("Start an async job to compute a path using feature data"); neither the Lua nor the doc states what terrain data that job reads internally, and the obstacle set is whatever the terrain's MAK_OBSTACLE feature query returns - contents not stated. Absence of an argument is evidence about the call signature, not about the planner's internal inputs. Per the rule, the text does not say it: not stated. (3) "used everywhere there is no navigation data" is a weaker reading than the file shows - per lines 5-9 and the tree at 1564, computePathThroughFeatures runs for every move-to; nav-mesh planning only refines off-road parts when available. Scope check passes: EntityLevel model set, header line 1 "This is the scripted task that ground vehicles use for all movement to a specified location." A narrowed meaning that would hold: "the Lua call site passes no slope or soil parameter, and the documented parameter table has none."

The feature planner is in fact the FIRST stage for every move (planPath is the top-level plan job, referenced at line 1564); the nav mesh is used only to refine off-feature parts (calcOffroadNavPath / vrf:findPathToLocation, lines 485-500). Vendor API doc (vrf.html:1591-1609) lists the complete parameter table as exactly start, destination, buffer, obstacleQuery, pathQuery, returnMultiPath, and describes the result parts as "on-feature"/"off-feature" ... quote:
Instances of DtFormationableSubordinatePredicate are used to determine 
whether a subordinate is capable part of a formation 
(i.e. it can move and its not embarked).

quote:
A route is a control object that 
contains an ordered list of vertices that represent a path for the entity
to follow. Entities that implement this task move to the first vertex, 
then move successively from one vertex to the next. The task is considered
complete when the entity reaches the last vertex in the route.
meaning: Confirms verbatim the citation this project's fix (DropOriginVertexMeters) relied on: the vendor's own move-along semantics are 'go to vertex 0 first, then the rest' -- so a route whose vertex 0 is the unit's original (pre-spread) coordinate will always send the entity back there first, exactly as the project inferred.

verdict.objection: The quote is verbatim (lines 26-30, mid-line 26 onward), but the 'meaning' over-reads it on the word "always" and on "vertex 0". Two qualifiers in the same header contradict the unconditional claim: (a) lines 91-94, "Flag indicating whether traversal should start at the beginning of route / or at the closest point (which may be somewhere along the route).  Beginning / is either 1st or last vertex, depending on traversal direction.  By default, / startAtClosestPoint is false." So the doc's "first vertex" is direction-dependent (traversalDirection, lines 82-88) and can be bypassed entirely (setStartAtClosestPoint). The prose semantics hold only for the DEFAULTS (traversalDirection false, startAtClosestPoint false) -- the header states those defaults, so a default-configured task does behave as the project inferred, but "will always send the entity back there first" is not supported. (b) lines 32-37 qualify who traverses: "Both individual and pseudo-aggregate entities implement this task. A / pseudo-aggregate entity forwards the move-along task to its lead / subordinate. All other subordinates in the pseudo-aggregate are tasked / to follow in formation." For a composed platoon/company, only the lead subordinate walks the vertices; the rest move in formation -- so the "entity returns to vertex 0" statement does not transfer unmodified to a composed unit. Scope check: the header never says ground vehicle, entity-level, or any domain -- it says "Entities" and "individual and pseudo-aggregate entities". It is not aggregate-level (DtAggregate) and not human/air-specific, but ground-vehicle applicability is not stated; it is inferred from the task being domain-generic.

The quote is verbatim (exact, including line breaks) at vrfmodel\groundMovementChooserController.h:30-38, and it is truncated in the finding - it continues "This controller can be fully removed once this level of compatibility is no longer required." The cited vrfobjcore\groundMovementChooserPSR.h:71-76 contains none of it; citing it makes the claim look doubly sourced when it is single-sourced. Anyone opening the PSR line range gets an unrelated subtask-flag comment.

  (a) "present in every ground movement sysdef" - FALSE as stated.
